what_it_does: High-level synthesis (HLS) is a tool that automatically converts an algorithm description into a chip blueprint — it lets designers explore many possible hardware implementations quickly. Approximate computing deliberately introduces small, acceptable errors in a chip's arithmetic to save power or area (for example, rounding aggressively). Combining these two ideas means evaluating a huge number of design variants, each of which must be fully approximated and simulated to know whether the accuracy loss is tolerable — and that exhaustive search takes too long. ADVISOR short-circuits this by computing a static score called the Approximation Friendliness Index (AFI) for each candidate design before doing any expensive simulation: a high score predicts the design will tolerate approximation well, so only those designs go through the full costly evaluation. The paper claims a 68x speedup over checking every variant.
